chapter.name: The World of Metals and Non-metals

questions.q: Copper, aluminium and iron look shiny. What is the shine shown by metals called?
questions.a: Metallic lustre. The chapter calls the lustre shown by metals metallic lustre; malleability, ductility and sonority are other properties of metals.

questions.q: Which metal is found in a liquid state at room temperature and is seen in some thermometers?
questions.a: Mercury. It is the one metal the chapter names as a liquid at room temperature; sodium is a soft solid, and aluminium and copper are hard solids.

questions.q: Match each material in Column I with its description in Column II. Column I: 1. Sodium  2. Gold  3. Coal  4. Wood. Column II: (p) neither malleable nor brittle  (q) a metal soft enough to be cut with a knife  (r) one of the two most malleable metals  (s) brittle; breaks into pieces when beaten.
questions.a: 1-q, 2-r, 3-s, 4-p: sodium can be cut with a knife, gold (with silver) is the most malleable metal, coal is brittle, and wood neither flattens nor breaks.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Once iron came into common use in India, ploughs made from iron were much superior to the ploughs used before. Reason (R): Iron, like copper and aluminium, shows metallic lustre.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true, but R does not explain A. Iron is lustrous (p. 43), but the chapter says iron ploughs were superior because of iron's strength (p. 44); shine does not make a plough work better.

questions.q: Define malleability and give one example of an everyday thing that is made because metals are malleable.
s: Malleability: the property by which materials can be beaten into thin sheets
Example: silver foil on sweets, or aluminium foil used to wrap food
questions.a: Malleability is the property by which materials can be beaten into thin sheets. Example: thin silver foil on sweets, or aluminium foil for wrapping food.

questions.q: True or False: All metals are hard solids. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: sodium and potassium are so soft that they can be cut with a knife, and mercury is a liquid at room temperature
questions.a: False. Some metals, such as sodium and potassium, are so soft that they can be cut with a knife, and mercury is a liquid at room temperature.

questions.q: Yashwant and Anandi visit Sudarshan uncle, an ironsmith. (a) Name two items of daily use that he makes. (b) Which material does he use for the handles, and what does he burn in his furnace? (c) Why does he beat the red-hot iron block with a hammer?
s: (a) Any two: flat pans (tawas), buckets, tongs, spades, axes, trowels, rakes
(b) Wood for the handles; coal in the furnace to heat the iron
(c) To shape it into a tool, such as an axe
questions.a: (a) Any two of tawas, buckets, tongs, spades, axes, trowels or rakes. (b) Handles are made of wood, and coal is used in the furnace to heat the iron. (c) He beats it to shape it into an axe (a tool).

questions.q: After filling Table 4.1 for copper, aluminium, an iron nail, sulfur, coal and a block of wood, Kiran writes: 'Every material in my table that is non-lustrous is also brittle.' Check her claim against the six objects and say whether it holds.
s: Non-lustrous objects in the table: sulfur, coal and wood
Sulfur and coal break into pieces (brittle), but wood neither flattens nor breaks, so it is not brittle
So the claim does not hold: wood is a non-lustrous material that is not brittle
questions.a: The claim does not hold. The non-lustrous objects are sulfur, coal and wood. Sulfur and coal are brittle, but wood neither gets flattened nor breaks into pieces, so it is neither malleable nor brittle.

questions.q: A Class 7 group in Udaipur repeats Activity 4.1. On a hard stone floor they place a copper strip, an aluminium strip, an iron nail, a pea-sized lump of sulfur and a piece of coal. They first note which objects shine, then strike each object once with a hammer under the teacher's supervision. The three metal objects shine and become flat; the sulfur and the coal look dull and break into pieces. (a) Which objects in the passage show metallic lustre? (b) Name the property shown by the objects that became flat. (c) What word describes the sulfur and the coal? (d) Which two metals does the chapter call the most malleable?
s: (a) The copper strip, the aluminium strip and the iron nail
(b) Malleability
(c) Brittle
(d) Gold and silver
questions.a: (a) The copper strip, the aluminium strip and the iron nail. (b) Malleability: they can be beaten into thin sheets. (c) Brittle: they break into pieces. (d) Gold and silver.

questions.q: A Class 7 group repeats Activity 4.1 with six pieces, each 4.0 square centimetres in area, and gives each piece 20 equal hammer blows. Their record: copper 6.0 cm2, no cracks; aluminium 8.0 cm2, no cracks; iron 4.6 cm2, no cracks; sulfur broke into pieces; coal broke into pieces; wood still 4.0 cm2, neither flattened nor broken. (a) Sort the six into malleable, brittle, and neither malleable nor brittle, using the record. (b) Work out the percentage increase in area for each metal and rank the metals from most to least spread. (c) From these six, which should be chosen to make a thin sheet for wrapping food, and does the record agree with the use the chapter gives? (d) Iron spread the least, yet Sudarshan uncle beats iron into axes and tawas. What does he do to the iron first, and why might he do this? (e) A student concludes, 'Iron spread least, so it is the weakest metal and would make the poorest plough.' Judge this conclusion.
s: (a) Malleable: copper, aluminium, iron (they flattened); brittle: sulfur, coal (broke into pieces); neither: wood (stayed the same, did not break)
(b) Copper (6.0-4.0)/4.0 = 50%, aluminium (8.0-4.0)/4.0 = 100%, iron (4.6-4.0)/4.0 = 15%; ranking aluminium > copper > iron
(c) Aluminium, the most spread in the record; this agrees with the chapter, where aluminium foil is used to wrap food because aluminium is malleable
(d) He heats the iron red hot in a coal furnace before beating it; any sensible reason for heating it first (for example, that it then shapes more easily) is accepted
(e) Wrong: spreading under the hammer measures malleability, not strength; the chapter says iron's strength made iron ploughs much superior to earlier ones
questions.a: (a) Malleable: copper, aluminium and iron; brittle: sulfur and coal; neither: wood. (b) Copper 50%, aluminium 100%, iron 15%, so aluminium spread most, then copper, then iron. (c) Aluminium, which matches the chapter's aluminium foil for wrapping food. (d) He heats the iron red hot in the coal furnace and then beats it; a sensible reason is that the hot iron is then easier to beat into shape (cold iron spread only 15% in the record). (e) The conclusion is wrong: how far a metal spreads shows malleability, not strength, and the chapter says ploughs of iron were much superior because of iron's strength.

questions.q: What is the property of materials by which they can be drawn into wires called?
questions.a: Ductility. Malleability is being beaten into sheets, sonority is producing a ringing sound, and conduction is the transfer of heat.

questions.q: Read the statements. Statement I: Metal wires are used in stringed musical instruments such as the veena and the sitar. Statement II: Coal can be drawn into thin wires. Statement III: A metal coin dropped on the floor produces a ringing sound. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements I and III are correct. Metal wires are used in the veena and sitar, and a metal coin rings when dropped; coal is not ductile, so it cannot be drawn into wires.

questions.q: Ria drops four objects from the same height and writes down the sound each makes: metal spoon - ringing; metal coin - dull; piece of coal - dull; block of wood - dull. Which entry is most likely a mistake?
questions.a: The coin entry. In Activity 4.2 the metal spoon and the metal coin both produce a ringing sound, while coal and wood produce dull sounds, so 'coin - dull' does not fit.

questions.q: What is sonority? Name two things from daily life whose ringing sound is due to it.
s: Sonority: the property of metals that enables them to produce a ringing sound
Any two: a school bell, ghungroos, a metal spoon, plate or coin dropped on the floor
questions.a: Sonority is the property of metals that enables them to produce a ringing sound. Examples: the school bell and ghungroos (or a metal spoon, plate or coin dropped on the floor).

questions.q: True or False: Coal and sulfur can be drawn into wires just like copper. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: coal and sulfur are not ductile; ductility is mainly possessed by metals such as copper
questions.a: False. Coal and sulfur are not ductile and no wires are made of them; the property of being drawn into wires is mainly possessed by metals such as copper.

questions.q: A Kathak dancer wears metal ghungroos on her ankles, and her brother plays a guitar with metal strings. (a) Name the property of metals that makes each possible. (b) A friend suggests making the ghungroos from small beads of hard dry wood instead. Would they ring in the same way? Give a reason.
s: (a) Ghungroos: sonority (ringing sound); guitar strings: ductility (metal drawn into wires)
(b) No: wood is not sonorous and gives a dull sound when struck, unlike metal
questions.a: (a) The ghungroos ring because metals are sonorous; the guitar strings are metal wires, possible because metals are ductile. (b) No. Wood produces a dull sound, not a ringing one, so wooden beads would not ring like metal ghungroos.

questions.q: Give one use from the chapter for each of these: (a) copper or aluminium wire, (b) metal wires in ornaments (name two such ornaments), (c) ropes made of steel wires.
s: (a) Electrical fittings (wiring)
(b) Any two: bangles, necklaces, earrings
(c) Suspension bridges, or cranes that lift heavy objects
questions.a: (a) Electrical fittings. (b) Ornaments such as bangles, necklaces and earrings are made from metal wires. (c) Suspension bridges and cranes, because steel ropes can support heavy loads.

questions.q: In Activity 4.2 a metal spoon, a coin, a piece of coal and a block of wood are dropped 'from a certain height'. (a) Why should all four be dropped from the same height? (b) What result shows that the spoon and the coin are sonorous? (c) Why are coal and wood included in the activity at all?
s: (a) So that only the material changes; a different height could change the sound and make the comparison unfair
(b) The spoon and the coin produce a ringing sound
(c) They give a dull sound to compare against, showing that the ringing sound is a property of the metals
questions.a: (a) Keeping the height the same means any difference in sound comes from the material, not from how far it fell. (b) The spoon and coin give a ringing sound. (c) Coal and wood give dull sounds, a comparison that shows the ringing is special to metals (sonority).

questions.q: A craft group in Puri wants to make a wind chime that rings in the breeze, to hang on an open balcony facing the sea. They can choose from wooden sticks, plain iron rods and copper tubes. (a) Why would wooden sticks make a poor chime? (b) Plain iron rods ring well. Why might they still be a poor choice for this balcony? (c) What change does the chapter say appears on copper objects kept open in the air? (d) Recommend one of the three materials and give two reasons from the chapter.
s: (a) Wood is not sonorous: it gives a dull sound, not a ringing one
(b) The sea-facing balcony has moist air (air and water), so plain iron would rust
(c) A green coating forms on copper (corrosion)
(d) Copper tubes: metal, so sonorous and rings; does not rust like iron (accept iron rods only if a protection such as painting is added, with two chapter-based reasons)
questions.a: (a) Wood gives a dull sound because it is not sonorous. (b) Moist sea air gives iron both air and water, so plain iron rods would rust. (c) Copper objects get a green coating, a form of corrosion. (d) Copper tubes: as a metal, copper is sonorous and rings, and it does not rust as iron does, though it may slowly get a green coating.

questions.q: Meenu's kitchen and home have: a tea strainer made of metal wire, a gold chain, a metal bell at the door, a steel spoon and a wooden rolling pin. (a) Which property of metals lets the tea strainer be made from metal wire? (b) How long a wire can one gram of gold be drawn into? (c) Which property of metals makes the door bell ring? (d) Meenu drops the steel spoon and the wooden rolling pin on the floor. Which one gives a ringing sound? (e) Could the tea strainer be made from wires of coal? Give a reason.
s: (a) Ductility
(b) About 2 kilometres
(c) Sonority
(d) The steel spoon; wood gives a dull sound
(e) No: coal is not ductile, it cannot be drawn into wires
questions.a: (a) Ductility. (b) A 2 km long wire. (c) Sonority. (d) The steel spoon rings; the wooden rolling pin gives a dull sound. (e) No, because coal is not ductile and cannot be drawn into wires.

questions.q: What is the transfer of heat from one point to another of a material called?
questions.a: Conduction. Materials that transfer heat in this way are called conductors.

questions.q: Match each item in Column I with the material and reason in Column II. Column I: 1. Cooking vessel  2. Handle of the cooking vessel  3. Electrician's gloves  4. Wire in a tester circuit. Column II: (p) rubber, a poor conductor of electricity  (q) copper, a good conductor of electricity  (r) metal, a good conductor of heat  (s) wood, a poor conductor of heat.
questions.a: 1-r, 2-s, 3-p, 4-q: vessels are metal because metals conduct heat well, handles are wood which conducts heat poorly, gloves are rubber which is a poor conductor of electricity, and copper wire conducts electricity.

questions.q: Assertion (A): In Activity 4.3, the upper end of the metal spoon becomes hotter than the upper end of the wooden spoon. Reason (R): The metal spoon and the wooden spoon used are of almost the same size and thickness.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true, but R does not explain A. Taking spoons of the same size and thickness only makes the comparison fair; the metal spoon gets hotter because metal conducts heat well and wood conducts it poorly.

questions.q: True or False: In Activity 4.4, all the materials that made the bulb of the tester glow were metals. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: aluminium foil, the iron nail and the copper wire made the bulb glow, while sulfur, coal, wood, stone, the rubber eraser and nylon rope did not
questions.a: True. Only aluminium, iron and copper made the bulb glow; sulfur, coal, wood, stone, the eraser and the nylon rope did not, so every material that lit the bulb was a metal.

questions.q: Why are cooking vessels mostly made of metal, while their handles are made of wood or similar materials?
s: Metals are good conductors of heat, so the vessel passes heat to the food
Wood is a poor conductor of heat, so the handle stays cool enough to hold
questions.a: Metals are good conductors of heat, so a metal vessel heats the food well. Wood does not conduct heat well, so a wooden handle stays safe to hold.

questions.q: Meera wants to find out whether a steel spoon conducts electricity. (a) How can she use the tester circuit from the chapter to test it? (b) What result should she expect, and why?
s: (a) Place the steel spoon in the gap of the tester circuit (touching both free ends) and see whether the bulb glows
(b) The bulb should glow, because the spoon is a metal object (steel is a mixture of iron and carbon) and metals are good conductors of electricity
questions.a: (a) Put the spoon in the gap between the two free wire ends of the tester and watch the bulb. (b) The bulb should glow: the spoon is a metal object (steel contains iron), and in Activity 4.4 the metal objects made the bulb glow.

questions.q: In Activity 4.3, a metal spoon and a wooden spoon are kept in hot water for a few minutes. (a) Which spoon's upper end feels hotter? (b) What does this tell us about the metal? (c) What does it tell us about the wood?
s: (a) The metal spoon
(b) Metal is a good conductor of heat; heat travels through it to the upper end
(c) Wood is a poor conductor of heat
questions.a: (a) The metal spoon. (b) Heat travels through the metal spoon, so metal is a good conductor of heat. (c) The wooden spoon transfers heat poorly, so wood is a poor conductor of heat.

questions.q: Kavya clips the two ends of her tester onto a copper wire that still has its plastic covering on; the bulb does not glow. She then clips them onto an aluminium foil strip and onto an iron nail; the bulb glows both times. She concludes, 'Copper is a poor conductor of electricity, so it is not a metal like aluminium and iron.' (a) Find what went wrong in her copper test. (b) What result does the chapter report for a copper wire in the tester? (c) How should she repeat the test, and what should she then conclude about copper?
s: (a) The clips touched only the plastic covering, which is a poor conductor of electricity, so no electricity could reach the copper
(b) In Activity 4.4 a copper wire makes the bulb glow: copper, like aluminium and iron, is a good conductor of electricity
(c) Remove the plastic from the two ends and clip onto the bare copper; the bulb glows, so copper is a good conductor and her conclusion is wrong
questions.a: (a) The clips touched only the plastic covering, and plastic is a poor conductor of electricity, so electricity never reached the copper. (b) The chapter reports that a copper wire makes the tester bulb glow, just as aluminium and iron do. (c) She should strip the plastic off the two ends and clip onto the bare copper; the bulb will glow, showing copper is a good conductor of electricity (a metal), so her conclusion is wrong.

questions.q: Ramesh runs a tea stall at a bus stand in Pune. He boils tea in an aluminium pan that has a wooden handle. Above the stove a bulb hangs from a copper wire covered with plastic, and it glows as soon as he switches it on each evening. (a) Why does the aluminium pan heat the tea well? (b) Why is the pan's handle made of wood? (c) The bulb glows when switched on. What does this show about copper, and which other property of copper lets it be made into this wire? (d) His helper says the plastic on the copper wire is only for colour. Is he right? Explain.
s: (a) Aluminium is a metal, a good conductor of heat
(b) Wood is a poor conductor of heat, so the handle stays safe to hold
(c) Copper is a good conductor of electricity; it can be drawn into wires because it is ductile
(d) No: plastic is a poor conductor of electricity, so the covering protects people from electric shock
questions.a: (a) Aluminium is a metal and conducts heat well. (b) Wood conducts heat poorly, so the handle does not get too hot to hold. (c) Electricity flows through the copper wire to the bulb, so copper is a good conductor of electricity; it can be made into a wire because it is ductile. (d) No. Plastic is a poor conductor of electricity, so the covering protects anyone who touches the wire from an electric shock.

questions.q: A class stands five rods of equal size in the same hot water and times how long the top end takes to feel warm. Copper: 40 s. Aluminium: 55 s. Iron: 150 s. Wood: still cool after 10 minutes. Plastic: still cool after 10 minutes. In a tester, copper, aluminium and iron make the bulb glow; wood and plastic do not. (a) Sort the five into good and poor conductors of heat, using the data. (b) How many times as long did iron take as copper? (c) A cook wants the base of a pot that passes heat to food fastest. Which of the five should she choose, and why? (d) The pot will sit on an electric hot plate. Both wood and plastic stayed cool; does the tester data help her choose between them for the handle? Explain. (e) A student says, 'Iron took nearly four times as long as copper, so iron is a poor conductor of heat, like wood.' Judge this claim using the data.
s: (a) Good conductors of heat: copper, aluminium, iron; poor: wood, plastic
(b) 150 / 40 = 3.75 times as long
(c) Copper: its top end warmed fastest (40 s), so it passed heat best
(d) No: neither wood nor plastic made the bulb glow, so both are poor conductors of heat and of electricity; the data cannot separate them, and either is safe for the handle
(e) Wrong: iron warmed in 150 s while wood stayed cool after 600 s, and iron lit the bulb; iron is a good conductor, only slower than copper in this test
questions.a: (a) Copper, aluminium and iron are good conductors of heat; wood and plastic are poor ones. (b) 150 / 40 = 3.75, so iron took 3.75 times as long. (c) Copper, because its top end warmed fastest, so it passes heat best. (d) No. Both stayed cool and both kept the bulb off, so both are poor conductors of heat and electricity; the data does not separate them, and either would make a safe handle. (e) The claim is wrong: iron's top end warmed in 150 s while wood was still cool after 10 minutes (600 s), and iron made the bulb glow; iron is a good conductor of heat, just slower than copper here.

questions.q: What is the brown deposit that forms on iron objects kept in moist air called?
questions.a: Rust. The process by which rust forms on iron objects is called rusting.

questions.q: In galvanisation, iron is protected from rusting by applying a layer of which metal?
questions.a: Zinc. Galvanisation means applying a protective layer of zinc metal on iron.

questions.q: Assertion (A): After 8-10 days, the iron nail in bottle B of Activity 4.5 shows no brown deposit. Reason (R): The silica gel placed in bottle A makes the air in that bottle dry.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true but R does not explain A. The silica gel is in bottle A, not bottle B. The nail in bottle B stays free of rust because it is in boiled and cooled water under a layer of oil, so it has water but no air.

questions.q: True or False: Only iron gets damaged when metals are kept open in the atmosphere. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: other metals also discolour; copper gets a green coating and silver a black coating, and this damage is called corrosion
questions.a: False. Many other metals also get discoloured in the open, such as copper (green coating) and silver (black coating). Gradual damage of metal surfaces like this is called corrosion.

questions.q: A coastal town spends money every year to repair the iron railings along its sea front. (a) Name the process that damages the railings and the two things it needs. (b) Explain why painting the railings can reduce this spending.
s: (a) Rusting; it needs both air and water (moist air)
(b) Paint covers the iron, keeping moist air away from it, so less rust forms and fewer railings need repair
questions.a: (a) Rusting, which needs both air and water. (b) Painting is a method of preventing rusting: the paint layer keeps moist air off the iron, so less damage happens and less money is spent on repairs.

questions.q: (a) What is rusting? (b) What is corrosion? (c) What colour of coating forms on copper objects, and what colour on silver objects?
s: (a) Rusting: the process of formation of rust (a brown deposit) on objects made of iron
(b) Corrosion: gradual deterioration of metal surfaces caused by air, water or other substances
(c) Copper: green coating; silver: black coating
questions.a: (a) Rusting is the formation of the brown deposit called rust on iron objects. (b) Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of metal surfaces caused by air, water or other substances. (c) Green on copper, black on silver.

questions.q: Rahul set up Activity 4.5. After 10 days the nail in bottle C had rusted as expected, but the nail in bottle A, kept with silica gel, also showed brown spots. Suggest two mistakes in setting up bottle A that could explain this, and say how each could let the brown spots appear.
s: Mistake 1: the cap of bottle A was not tight, so moist air from outside could reach the nail
Mistake 2: an old nail was not scrubbed with sandpaper, so brown deposits were already on it (or too little silica gel to keep the air dry)
Explanation: rust needs both air and water, so dry air alone in bottle A should give no brown deposit
questions.a: Bottle A should have dry air only, and rust needs both air and water. Possible mistakes: (1) the cap was loose, letting moist air in; (2) an old nail was used without scrubbing off its brown deposits with sandpaper, or there was not enough silica gel to keep the air dry.

questions.q: A family wants to protect four iron things in their house from rusting: a front gate, the chain of a bicycle, a water bucket and the hinges of a door. Suggest a suitable method from the chapter (painting, oiling, greasing or galvanisation) for each item, using at least three different methods in all.
s: Front gate: any suitable method from the chapter (for example painting or galvanisation)
Bicycle chain: any suitable method (for example oiling or greasing)
Water bucket: any suitable method (for example galvanisation or painting)
Door hinges: any suitable method (for example greasing or oiling), with at least three different methods used across the four items
questions.a: Any suitable method for each, with at least three different methods in all. For example: gate - painting; bicycle chain - oiling; bucket - galvanisation (a layer of zinc); hinges - greasing. Each method keeps moist air away from the iron.

questions.q: A class in Kochi sets up four bottles with clean iron nails and checks them after 10 days. Bottle P: nail with silica gel, tightly capped - no brown deposit. Bottle Q: nail fully under freshly boiled and cooled water with a layer of oil, capped - no brown deposit. Bottle R: plain nail partly in water, bottle open - brown deposit all over the wet part by day 3. Bottle S: a nail painted all over, then scratched once through the paint, partly in water, bottle open - by day 10 a thin brown line only along the scratch. (a) Which two bottles show that rusting needs both air and water, and how? (b) Explain why S rusted only along the scratch. (c) Anu says, 'S rusted too, so painting is useless.' Judge her claim using R and S. (d) Rank the nails from least to most rust and name the one condition that decides the order.
s: (a) P and Q: P had dry air only and Q had water only, and neither rusted
(b) The paint keeps moist air off the iron; at the scratch the iron was in contact with both air and water, so rust formed there only

(c) Wrong: under the same conditions R rusted all over its wet part by day 3, while the painted surface of S stayed free of rust for 10 days; paint works where it is unbroken, so scratches should be repainted
(d) P and Q (no rust), then S (a thin line), then R (most); decided by how much iron surface is in contact with both air and water
questions.a: (a) P and Q: dry air alone (P) and water alone (Q) gave no rust. (b) Paint keeps air and water away from the iron; along the scratch the iron met both, so it rusted only there. (c) Her claim is wrong: R rusted all over its wet part by day 3, but S rusted only along the scratch in 10 days, so paint protects the iron wherever it is unbroken; the scratch should be repainted. (d) P and Q (no rust), then S, then R; the order is set by how much of the iron is exposed to both air and water.

questions.q: Lakshmi lives in a fishing village by the sea. She notes three iron chairs after the monsoon, all on the same open verandah. Chair 1, galvanised: no rust. Chair 2, plain iron: covered with brown deposit. Chair 3, plain iron that had been painted: no rust except at two spots where the paint had chipped off, which are brown. (a) Why did chair 2 rust? (b) What does comparing chairs 1 and 2 suggest? (c) Why did chair 3 rust only at the chipped spots? (d) A neighbour says, 'Chair 1 stayed clean only because it was bought later than chair 2.' Lakshmi's notes do not give the dates. Judge whether her comparison of chairs 1 and 2 can rule out his idea, and say how to check it. (e) Recommend what she should do with chair 2 before the next monsoon, with a reason.
s: (a) On the open verandah it got moist air, both air and water, which causes rusting
(b) Both stood in the same place, so the zinc layer (galvanisation) appears to have protected chair 1
(c) The paint keeps moist air away from the iron; at the chipped spots the iron is open to both air and water, so it rusts there
(d) It cannot rule it out: age is a second difference between the chairs; compare chairs of the same age, one galvanised and one plain, kept side by side
(e) Remove the rust and paint it (or oil/grease it), or keep it in a dry place, so moist air cannot reach the iron
questions.a: (a) The open verandah by the sea exposed it to moist air, and rust needs both air and water. (b) Chairs 1 and 2 stood in the same place, so galvanisation (a zinc layer) seems to have prevented rust. (c) Paint keeps air and water from reaching the iron; where it chipped off, moist air reached the iron and rust formed only there. (d) Her notes cannot rule it out: if the chairs differ in age too, the comparison is not fair. Comparing a galvanised and a plain chair of the same age, side by side, would settle it. (e) Clean it and paint (or grease) it, or store it in a dry place, so that air and water cannot both reach the iron.

questions.q: What is seen when a clean magnesium ribbon is burnt in air?
o: It burns with a dazzling white flame and changes into a white powder
It burns with a blue flame and changes into a black powder
It melts into a silvery liquid without burning
It gives off a gas and leaves nothing behind
questions.a: It burns with a dazzling white flame and changes into a white powder, magnesium oxide.

questions.q: In which liquid is sodium stored?
questions.a: Kerosene. Sodium reacts vigorously with oxygen and water, so it is kept in kerosene to keep it away from air and moisture.

questions.q: Read the statements. Statement I: Phosphorus is stored in water because it catches fire when exposed to air. Statement II: Sulfur reacts with water to form sulfurous acid directly. Statement III: Plastic and glass are not classified as metals or non-metals because they are not elements. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements I and III are correct. Sulfur shows no reaction with water; sulfurous acid forms only when sulfur dioxide (from burning sulfur) is dissolved in water.

questions.q: Match each substance in Column I with the correct statement in Column II. Column I: 1. Solution of magnesium oxide  2. Sulfur dioxide dissolved in water  3. Sodium  4. Phosphorus. Column II: (p) stored in kerosene  (q) turns red litmus blue  (r) stored in water  (s) forms sulfurous acid and turns blue litmus red.
questions.a: 1-q, 2-s, 3-p, 4-r: magnesium oxide solution is basic, sulfur dioxide in water gives sulfurous acid, sodium is kept in kerosene and phosphorus is kept in water.

questions.q: True or False: A solution of magnesium oxide in water turns red litmus paper blue. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: magnesium oxide is the oxide of a metal and is basic in nature; oxides of metals are generally basic
questions.a: True. Magnesium oxide is a metal oxide, and its solution is basic, so it turns red litmus blue. Generally, oxides of metals are basic.

questions.q: Nisha burns a magnesium ribbon, mixes the white powder with warm water and dips only a blue litmus paper in it. The paper stays blue. She writes, 'So the solution is basic.' (a) Is one blue paper enough to show this? Give a reason. (b) Which paper should she also use, and what change in it shows that the solution is basic?
s: (a) No: blue litmus stays blue in a basic solution and also in a neutral one, so this result alone cannot show the solution is basic
(b) Red litmus paper: it turns blue in the magnesium oxide solution, which shows it is basic
questions.a: (a) No. A blue litmus paper stays blue whether the solution is basic or neutral, so it does not settle the question. (b) She should dip a red litmus paper; the magnesium oxide solution turns it blue, which shows the solution is basic.

questions.q: In Activity 4.6 a magnesium ribbon is burnt and the product is tested. (a) Name the white powder formed. (b) What does magnesium react with to form it? (c) What effect does its solution have on red litmus paper?
s: (a) Magnesium oxide
(b) Oxygen present in the air
(c) It turns red litmus blue (it is basic)
questions.a: (a) Magnesium oxide. (b) Oxygen in the air. (c) It turns red litmus paper blue, showing it is basic.

questions.q: Two watch glasses hold solutions made by burning an element in air and mixing the product with water. One element was magnesium and the other was sulfur. Solution A turns red litmus paper blue; solution B turns blue litmus paper red. (a) Which solution came from magnesium? Give a reason. (b) Name the gas formed when the other element burnt and the acid it formed in water. (c) What general rule about the oxides of metals and of non-metals do the two results show?
s: (a) Solution A: magnesium oxide in water is basic and turns red litmus blue
(b) Sulfur formed sulfur dioxide gas, which forms sulfurous acid in water
(c) Oxides of metals are basic; oxides of non-metals are acidic
questions.a: (a) Solution A came from magnesium, since magnesium oxide gives a basic solution that turns red litmus blue. (b) Burning sulfur gives sulfur dioxide gas, which dissolves in water to form sulfurous acid (solution B, acidic). (c) Metal oxides are basic and non-metal oxides are acidic.

questions.q: In Activity 4.7 the teacher burns powdered sulfur in a deflagrating spoon inside a gas jar, keeps the jar covered with a lid for 3-4 minutes, then adds a little water and shakes it. (a) Why must this activity be done in a fume hood or a well-ventilated area? (b) Why is the jar covered with a lid? (c) Why is the water shaken in the closed jar? (d) What result is seen with litmus, and what does it tell us about the oxides of non-metals?
s: (a) Burning sulfur produces gases that can be harmful if inhaled
(b) So that the gas produced (sulfur dioxide) does not escape
(c) So that the gas dissolves in the water
(d) The solution turns blue litmus red (acidic); oxides of non-metals are acidic
questions.a: (a) The gases from burning sulfur can be harmful to breathe. (b) The lid keeps the sulfur dioxide gas from escaping. (c) Shaking dissolves the gas in the water, forming sulfurous acid. (d) Blue litmus turns red, so the solution is acidic: the oxides of non-metals are acidic.

questions.q: A lab sheet describes two elements not named in the chapter. Element Q is shiny, can be beaten into sheets and drawn into wires, and makes the tester bulb glow. Element R is dull, breaks into pieces when hammered and does not make the bulb glow. (a) Classify Q and R as metal or non-metal, with one reason each. (b) Predict the effect of Q's oxide solution on litmus. (c) Predict the effect of R's oxide solution on litmus. (d) Ravi says, 'Q is a metal, so it is safe to keep it in water.' Judge his claim using an example from the chapter. (e) Ravi also says, 'R is a non-metal, so it must react with water.' Judge this claim.
s: (a) Q is a metal (lustrous, malleable, ductile, conducts electricity); R is a non-metal (dull, brittle, poor conductor)
(b) Q's oxide is expected to be basic: it turns red litmus blue
(c) R's oxide is expected to be acidic: it turns blue litmus red
(d) Not safe to assume: sodium is a metal that reacts vigorously with water and is stored in kerosene, so Q must be tested first
(e) Wrong: generally non-metals do not react with water (sulfur shows no reaction)
questions.a: (a) Q is a metal (shiny, malleable, ductile, a good conductor); R is a non-metal (dull, brittle, a poor conductor). (b) Q's oxide should be basic and turn red litmus blue. (c) R's oxide should be acidic and turn blue litmus red. (d) Ravi's claim is unsafe: sodium is a metal that reacts vigorously with water, so being a metal does not make Q safe in water. (e) Wrong: non-metals generally do not react with water; sulfur shows no reaction.

questions.q: Which non-metal is commonly used in the purification of water?
questions.a: Chlorine. Iodine solution is used on wounds, nitrogen in fertilisers, and carbon is the building block of life.

questions.q: According to the chapter, which special metal is used in atomic energy and which in aerospace?
o: Zirconium in atomic energy, titanium in aerospace
Titanium in atomic energy, zirconium in aerospace
Aluminium in atomic energy, iron in aerospace
Iron in atomic energy, aluminium in aerospace
questions.a: Zirconium is used in atomic energy and titanium in aerospace; iron and aluminium are the metals the chapter says are recycled in India.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Chlorine is commonly used in the purification of water. Reason (R): Non-metals are generally poor conductors of heat and electricity.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true, but R does not explain A. Chlorine is a non-metal used in water purification (p. 54), and non-metals are generally poor conductors (p. 53), but poor conduction has nothing to do with cleaning water.

questions.q: True or False: Carbon is a non-metal that is essential for all living things. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: carbon is the building block of all life forms and a key component of proteins, fats and carbohydrates
questions.a: True. Carbon is the building block of all life forms and a key part of proteins, fats and carbohydrates, which are needed for growth and energy.

questions.q: Name the non-metal that is (a) applied on wounds as a solution to act as an antiseptic, (b) used in making fertilisers.
s: (a) Iodine
(b) Nitrogen
questions.a: (a) Iodine (a solution of iodine is an antiseptic). (b) Nitrogen.

questions.q: A jeweller melts gold and copper together to make the metal for a set of bangles. (a) Using the chapter's meaning of an alloy, is the bangle metal an alloy? Give a reason. (b) Is the bangle metal an element? Use the chapter's meaning of an element.
s: (a) Yes: an alloy is a mixture of two or more metals (or a metal and a non-metal), and this is a mixture of two metals, gold and copper
(b) No: an element cannot be broken down into simpler substances, but this metal is a mixture of two elements, gold and copper
questions.a: (a) Yes. The chapter calls a mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal and a non-metal, an alloy; gold mixed with copper is a mixture of two metals. (b) No. An element cannot be broken down into simpler substances, whereas this is a mixture made of two elements.

questions.q: Give one use or role in everyday life of each of these non-metals: (a) oxygen, (b) nitrogen, (c) chlorine.
s: (a) Oxygen: we breathe it in; we cannot survive without it
(b) Nitrogen: used to make fertilisers; an essential nutrient for plant growth
(c) Chlorine: used in water purification
questions.a: (a) Oxygen is breathed in by us and is needed to survive. (b) Nitrogen is used to make fertilisers and is a nutrient for plants. (c) Chlorine is used to purify water.

questions.q: Dev sorts things in his room. He says, 'My glass tumbler and my plastic bottle are not shiny and do not conduct electricity, just like sulfur, so glass and plastic are non-metals.' (a) Metals and non-metals are sub-categories of which kind of substance? (b) Use the chapter's meaning of that word to show why Dev's claim is wrong. (c) Name two non-metals from the chapter, other than sulfur, that Dev could have listed instead.
s: (a) Elements
(b) An element cannot be broken down into simpler substances; glass and plastic are not elements, so the chapter does not classify them as metals or non-metals
(c) Any two of: phosphorus, oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, carbon (also chlorine, iodine)
questions.a: (a) Elements. (b) An element is a substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances; glass and plastic are not elements, so the chapter does not classify them as metals or non-metals, however dull or poorly conducting they are. (c) Any two of phosphorus, oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen and carbon (chlorine and iodine are also accepted).

questions.q: A farmer in Nashik tries a fertiliser containing nitrogen on three equal plots of the same crop. Plot P: fertiliser, watered daily, 30 kg of crop. Plot Q: no fertiliser, watered weekly, 18 kg. Plot R: fertiliser, watered weekly, 27 kg. (a) What does the chapter say nitrogen does for plants? (b) Which two plots make a fair test of the fertiliser alone? Work out the percentage increase it gave. (c) His son compares P with Q and says, 'The fertiliser raised the crop by 12 kg.' Judge this claim. (d) By what percentage of R's crop is P's crop larger, and which single change explains it?
s: (a) Nitrogen is an essential nutrient for the growth of plants (it is used to make fertilisers)
(b) R and Q: they differ only in fertiliser; (27-18)/18 = 50% increase
(c) Not fair: P and Q differ in both fertiliser and watering, so the 12 kg cannot all be credited to the fertiliser; the fair test shows 9 kg
(d) (30-27)/27 = about 11%; P and R differ only in watering (daily instead of weekly)
questions.a: (a) Nitrogen is an essential nutrient for plant growth, which is why it is used in fertilisers. (b) Plots R and Q, which differ only in the fertiliser: (27 - 18)/18 = 50%. (c) The claim is not fair, because P and Q differ in watering as well as fertiliser; the fair comparison R vs Q shows 9 kg from the fertiliser. (d) (30 - 27)/27 = about 11%; the only difference between P and R is daily instead of weekly watering.

questions.q: A town is repairing a small suspension footbridge over a river. Test data for ropes of equal thickness: copper wire rope breaks at 350 kg, aluminium wire rope at 250 kg, steel wire rope at 1,100 kg and a coir rope at 150 kg. Each rope on the bridge carries 400 kg, and the safety rule is that a rope must hold at least twice its load. (a) Which rope or ropes meet the rule? Show the check. (b) Steel is a mixture of which metal and which non-metal, and what does the chapter call such a mixture? (c) Why can metals and steel be made into wire ropes, while coal cannot? (d) The old ropes, made of steel wire, are to be thrown away as waste. What does the chapter say India does with iron, and why should the town follow it? (e) The old ropes had rusted most near the water. Suggest one way to protect the new ropes, with a reason.
s: (a) Needed: 2 x 400 = 800 kg; only steel (1,100 kg) meets it; copper 350, aluminium 250 and coir 150 kg all fall short (they cannot even carry 400 kg)
(b) Iron (metal) and carbon (non-metal); a mixture of a metal and a non-metal is an alloy
(c) Metals are ductile and can be drawn into wires; coal is not ductile (it is brittle)
(d) Iron is recycled in India to minimise waste and help sustainability, so the old steel ropes should go for recycling
(e) Paint, oil or grease the ropes so that moist air (air and water together) cannot reach the iron, since rust needs both
questions.a: (a) The rope must hold 2 x 400 = 800 kg; only the steel rope (1,100 kg) does. (b) Iron and carbon; such a mixture of a metal and a non-metal is an alloy. (c) Metals are ductile and can be drawn into wires, but coal is not ductile. (d) In India iron is recycled to minimise waste and for sustainability, so the old steel ropes should be recycled, not dumped. (e) Grease, oil or paint them, so that air and water cannot both reach the iron; rusting needs both.
